The Impressionist movement in art history is often characterized by its focus on capturing fleeting moments and the effects of light. However, many critics at the time dismissed Impressionist works as unfinished or lacking in substance. In most cases, Impressionist painters deliberately chose to paint en plein air, or outdoors, to better observe natural changes in light and atmosphere. This approach contrasted sharply with the academic tradition, which emphasized careful planning and studio work.

The Impressionists’ use of quick, visible brushstrokes was not merely a stylistic choice; it was a response to the challenge of depicting transient scenes before the light changed. Paradoxically, although their methods appeared spontaneous, many Impressionists carefully composed their works in advance, often returning to the same location multiple times. Some scholars argue that this blend of apparent immediacy and underlying structure is what gives Impressionist paintings their enduring appeal. Thus, while the movement was initially controversial, its innovative techniques have had a lasting impact on the trajectory of modern art.

In most cases, cognitive dissonance arises when individuals hold two conflicting beliefs or attitudes. However, not all instances of dissonance lead to changes in behavior or thought. Some people are able to tolerate a certain level of psychological discomfort without taking action. The classic example involves a person who values health but continues to smoke; the tension between belief and action can prompt either a change in behavior or a rationalization.

Paradoxically, research has shown that the greater the effort someone invests in a decision, the more likely they are to justify that decision, even if it conflicts with their prior beliefs. This effect is not limited to major life choices; it can be observed in everyday situations, such as consumer purchases. The cause-effect relationship between dissonance and attitude change is complex: while some individuals resolve dissonance by altering their beliefs, others may simply avoid situations that trigger discomfort. Thus, while many people experience cognitive dissonance, the ways in which they respond to it are varied and context-dependent.
